performers: Lukas Foss, piano; Philharmonic-Symphony Orchestra of New York; Leonard Bernstein
recorded: 27 February 1950, New York; issued as Columbia ML 4325
intro: Part II of the Second Symphony, The Age of Anxiety, in the original 1949 version, comprising the Dirge, the Masque for piano and percussion, and an Epilogue in which the soloist plays only a closing chord. Lukas Foss was the soloist and Bernstein conducted, in a recording made in February 1950.

cues.title: The Dirge, Largo
cues.text: The Dirge opens Part II. It is a lament for the loss of a guiding father figure, the “colossal dad” of Auden’s poem. Bernstein wrote that it “employs, in a harmonic way, a twelve-tone row out of which the main theme evolves”, and that it has a contrasting middle section.
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s programme note for the first performance and the Office’s summary of the poem, both on the Leonard Bernstein Office page for the symphony. The Dirge is the first section of Part II in the transfer note’s section list. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety https://archive.org/details/ml-4325-bernstein-sym-2-ii
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Commission and dedication, 1949
cues.text: The Koussevitzky Foundation commissioned the symphony, and Bernstein dedicated it “in tribute” to Serge Koussevitzky, who conducted the first performance on 8 April 1949. Bernstein finished the Epilogue three weeks before that concert.
cues.evidence: Leonard Bernstein Office, page for Symphony No. 2: commission, dedication, première date and the three weeks before the première in which the Epilogue was finished. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety

cues.title: The Masque, Extremely fast
cues.text: The Masque is a scherzo for piano and percussion alone. Bernstein described its piano-jazz as by turns “nervous, sentimental, self-satisfied, vociferous”. In the poem it is the late-night party at Rosetta’s apartment.
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s programme note and the Office’s summary of the poem, on the Bernstein Office page. The start of the Masque at about 5:41 is given in the transfer note and agrees with a change in the audio at that point. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety https://archive.org/details/ml-4325-bernstein-sym-2-ii
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Orchestra enters before the Epilogue
cues.text: Near the end of the Masque the orchestra joins the piano and percussion for four bars of “hectic jazz”, in Bernstein’s description. The piano stops, and a pianino in the orchestra continues the Masque as the Epilogue begins.
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s programme note, quoted on the Bernstein Office page and printed on the back of the Columbia LP sleeve, places the orchestra’s four bars at the end of the Masque, before the Epilogue. The place in this recording is estimated from the change in the audio at the start of the Epilogue. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety

cues.title: The Epilogue, 1949 version
cues.text: In the Epilogue, marked Adagio, the strings join the winds’ repeated statements of “something pure”. In this version the piano does not play until a single chord at the end. Bernstein revised the finale in 1965 and gave the soloist a cadenza.
cues.evidence: Bernstein’s programme note and his 1965 explanation of the revision, on the Bernstein Office page; the Internet Archive transfer note identifies this recording as the original version. The transfer note gives the start as about 10:10; the audio changes at about 10:14, where the orchestra stops. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety https://archive.org/details/ml-4325-bernstein-sym-2-ii
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The single closing chord
cues.text: The soloist, a detached observer in Bernstein’s scheme, plays a single chord at the very end of the 1949 score. The Bernstein Office reports that Bernstein’s note takes the chord as a symbol of the unity of man and God.
cues.evidence: Leonard Bernstein Office, page for Symphony No. 2, account of the programme note for the Epilogue. https://leonardbernstein.com/works/view/16/symphony-no-2-the-age-of-anxiety
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Transfer by Bryan of The Shellackophile, from a mono LP

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Shellackophile blog post offering this transfer is dated 8 October 2012 and the Internet Archive item was added on 11 April 2022. Neither date is established as the date of transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: FLAC and VBR MP3 derivatives of a mono LP transfer
fields.note: Equalisation, noise reduction and speed correction are not documented. The research desk measured the pitch of the file at about A = 441 Hz, which is consistent with normal LP speed (inference from the audio).

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Copyrighted Bernstein composition; performance licences through Boosey & Hawkes, according to the Leonard Bernstein Office
fields.note: A phonogram term assessment does not clear the composition, an arrangement or a modern score edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: commercial publication before 1963; the LP ML 4325 was reviewed in The American Record Guide of January 1951
fields.note: The American Record Guide, January 1951, reviews Columbia ML 4325 at $4.85, and The New Records, March 1951, reviews both the LP and the 78-rpm album MM-946. The Internet Archive note gives first issue in March 1951, which the January 1951 review shows to be too late for the LP; Discogs dates the US LP to 1950. Any of these years is before 1963. The project’s eu-published-before-1963 rule applies: the former 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 2013 extension. This is not US or worldwide clearance, not a Creative Commons licence and not a US-government recording. Rights in the composition are separate.

composer.epithet: American conductor, pianist and composer, music director of the New York Philharmonic from 1958 to 1969 and composer of West Side Story and the Chichester Psalms.

quote.text: This will be our reply to violence: to make music more intensely, more beautifully, more devotedly than ever before.
quote.source: Bernstein, remarks at Madison Square Garden, 25 November 1963; printed in Findings (1982)

composer.background:
Leonard Bernstein was born on 25 August 1918 in Lawrence, Massachusetts, the eldest of three children of Samuel and Jennie Bernstein, Jewish immigrants from Ukraine. The family moved to Boston when he was a few months old, and his father sold hairdressing and beauty supplies. In the autumn of 1928 an aunt gave the family an upright piano, and the ten-year-old Leonard began to pick out songs on it. Samuel Bernstein, who wanted his son to join the business, agreed to lessons. The New Yorker reported in 1958 that he had said backstage at Tanglewood: “someday I suppose the books will say, ‘Lenny Bernstein had a father.’” In October 1932 Bernstein began lessons with Helen Coates, an assistant to the Boston pianist Heinrich Gebhard.

He attended Boston Latin School and entered Harvard in 1935, where his teachers included Walter Piston and Edward Burlingame Hill. In January 1937 he met the conductor Dimitri Mitropoulos at a reception and spent the following week at Mitropoulos’s Boston Symphony rehearsals. On 14 November of that year he met Aaron Copland at a dance recital in New York. He graduated in June 1939.
